::: {#thm-digit-count}
#### The function $d$ counts digits

Let $d$ be the function of @exm-digit-count.
For every natural number $n$,

$$
10^{d(n) - 1} \le n < 10^{d(n)},
$$

so $n$ has exactly $d(n)$ decimal digits.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

A natural number $n$ has $m$ digits exactly when $10^{m - 1} \le n < 10^m$,
since $10^{m - 1}$, which is 1 followed by $m - 1$ zeros, is the smallest natural number with $m$ digits,
and $10^m$, which is 1 followed by $m$ zeros, is the smallest with $m + 1$.
So the inequalities say that $n$ has $d(n)$ digits.

The recursive rule uses $d\paren{\floor{n / 10}}$, not $d(n - 1)$,
so we use strong induction (@def-strong-induction).
Let $n$ be a natural number,
and suppose the inequalities hold for every natural number less than $n$.

If $n \le 9$, then $d(n) = 1$, and $10^0 = 1 \le n < 10 = 10^1$.

If $n \ge 10$, let $q = \floor{n / 10}$.
Then $q \le n / 10 < q + 1$, so $10q \le n < 10q + 10$.
Also $q \ge 1$, since $n / 10 \ge 1$, and $q < n$,
so $q$ is a natural number less than $n$, and by the strong induction hypothesis

$$
10^{d(q) - 1} \le q < 10^{d(q)}.
$$

The recursive rule gives $d(n) = 1 + d(q)$.
For the lower bound,

$$
\ba
n
&\ge 10 q
\\&\ge 10 \cdot 10^{d(q) - 1}
&& \text{(strong induction hypothesis)}
\\&= 10^{d(q)}
\\&= 10^{d(n) - 1}.
&& \text{(} d(n) = 1 + d(q) \text{)}
\ea
$$

For the upper bound, $q$ and $10^{d(q)}$ are integers with $q < 10^{d(q)}$, so $q + 1 \le 10^{d(q)}$, and

$$
\ba
n
&< 10 (q + 1)
\\&\le 10 \cdot 10^{d(q)}
&& \text{(} q + 1 \le 10^{d(q)} \text{)}
\\&= 10^{d(q) + 1}
\\&= 10^{d(n)}.
&& \text{(} d(n) = 1 + d(q) \text{)}
\ea
$$

So the inequalities hold for $n$,
and by strong induction they hold for every natural number $n$.

:::

:::
